title: ACCA FR - Financial Reporting
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA FR syllabus study guide. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: According to the IASB Conceptual Framework, which qualitative characteristic makes information capable of making a difference in the decisions made by users of financial statements?
options: Relevance
Verifiability
Timeliness
Comparability
items.explanation: Relevance is the fundamental qualitative characteristic that makes information capable of making a difference in user decisions. Verifiability, timeliness and comparability are enhancing characteristics that support useful information but do not by themselves make it decision-useful.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which of the following is one of the three attributes that together make information a faithful representation?
options: Comparability
Completeness
Timeliness
Understandability
items.explanation: A faithful representation is complete, neutral and free from error. Comparability, timeliness and understandability are enhancing qualitative characteristics rather than attributes of faithful representation.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: The IASB Conceptual Framework identifies going concern as an underlying assumption of financial reporting. Which statement best describes the going concern assumption?
options: The financial statements are prepared using current replacement values
The entity will earn a profit in every reporting period
The entity will continue in operation for the foreseeable future
The entity will be liquidated within twelve months
items.explanation: Going concern assumes the entity will continue in operation for the foreseeable future, so assets and liabilities are recorded on a basis other than forced liquidation values. It does not guarantee profits or require replacement cost measurement.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which of the following best describes a liability?
options: A future obligation that the entity may choose to settle in cash
An excess of cumulative income over cumulative expenses
A resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events
A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events
items.explanation: A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource arising from past events. A resource controlled by the entity is an asset, while the other options describe an avoidable obligation or a residual measure of performance.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: Which body is responsible for developing and issuing International Financial Reporting Standards for use around the world?
options: The International Accounting Standards Board
The International Organization of Securities Commissions
The IFRS Foundation Trustees
The IFRS Interpretations Committee
items.explanation: The International Accounting Standards Board develops and issues IFRS Standards. The Trustees oversee and fund the organisation, the Interpretations Committee issues application guidance, and IOSCO is an association of securities regulators.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: When no IFRS Standard specifically applies to a transaction, which source should an accountant consult first in developing an accounting policy?
options: The most recent pronouncements of other standard-setting bodies
Requirements in IFRS Standards dealing with similar and related issues
Accepted industry practice for comparable entities
The accountant's own judgement alone
items.explanation: IAS 8 requires an entity first to look at IFRS Standards and Interpretations that deal with similar and related issues. Other standard-setting pronouncements and accepted practice are lower in the hierarchy, and judgement alone is the last resort.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: The IASB Conceptual Framework states that information is material if omitting, misstating or obscuring it could influence the decisions of primary users. Materiality is best described as which aspect of a qualitative characteristic?
options: An enhancing characteristic called timeliness
A constraint known as cost
The entity-specific aspect of relevance
A separate fundamental characteristic
items.explanation: Materiality is an entity-specific aspect of relevance, applied to the nature and magnitude of items. It is not a separate characteristic, and the cost constraint limits rather than defines materiality.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting
items.stem: IFRS 13 defines fair value for financial reporting. Which of the following best describes fair value?
options: The original cost of the asset less accumulated depreciation
The amount an entity expecting to use the asset would pay for it
A value based on the entity's own view of the asset's worth
The price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants
items.explanation: Fair value is the exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. It is a market-based measure, not original cost, entity-specific value in use, or management's subjective view.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - The Conceptual and Regulatory Framework for Financial Reporting

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: A machine costs 100,000, has an estimated residual value of 10,000 and a useful life of five years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the annual depreciation charge?
items.explanation: Straight-line depreciation is cost less residual value divided by useful life, so 100,000 minus 10,000 equals 90,000, divided by five gives 18,000. Ignoring the residual value would incorrectly give 20,000.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: A non-current asset is revalued upwards under IAS 16. Where should the increase be recognised when it reverses a previous downward revaluation that was charged to profit or loss?
options: In other comprehensive income as a revaluation surplus
In profit or loss as a gain
In retained earnings as a prior period adjustment
In the statement of financial position only, with no entry to income
items.explanation: IAS 16 requires the increase to be recognised in profit or loss to the extent that it reverses a revaluation decrease previously recognised in profit or loss. Any excess above that amount is taken to other comprehensive income.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: An entity replaces a major component of a piece of plant and capitalises the replacement cost under IAS 16. What must the entity do with the carrying amount of the part that has been replaced?
options: Reclassify it as an intangible asset
Continue to depreciate it alongside the new component
Derecognise it when the replacement occurs
Transfer it to inventory
items.explanation: IAS 16 requires the carrying amount of a replaced part to be derecognised when a new component is capitalised. Continuing to depreciate a removed part would double count the asset, and reclassification is not permitted.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IAS 38, how should expenditure on the development phase of an internally generated intangible asset be treated when all the capitalisation criteria are met?
options: It is capitalised only if the project is already profitable
It is recorded as a prepayment until sales begin
It is always expensed as incurred
It is capitalised as an intangible asset
items.explanation: IAS 38 requires development expenditure to be capitalised once the entity can demonstrate technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete, probable future benefits and reliable measurement. Research expenditure, by contrast, is always expensed.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: An entity holds a brand acquired in a business combination that has no foreseeable limit to the period over which it is expected to generate cash flows. How should the brand be treated under IAS 38?
options: Not amortised but tested annually for impairment
Written off immediately against retained earnings
Amortised over a maximum of ten years
Amortised over its estimated useful life
items.explanation: An intangible asset with an indefinite useful life is not amortised but is tested for impairment at least annually and whenever there is an indication of impairment. A finite-lived intangible would be amortised over its useful life.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: An asset with a carrying amount of 500,000 has a fair value less costs of disposal of 420,000 and a value in use of 450,000. What is the impairment loss under IAS 36?
options: Nil
items.explanation: The recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, so it is 450,000. The impairment loss is the carrying amount of 500,000 less the recoverable amount of 450,000, which is 50,000.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Inventory that cost 100,000 has a net realisable value of 85,000, and it is not covered by a firm sales contract. Under IAS 2, what amount should be recognised as the inventory write-down?
options: Nil
items.explanation: IAS 2 requires inventory to be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost of 100,000 less net realisable value of 85,000 gives a write-down of 15,000 recognised in profit or loss.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IAS 37, which of the following is required before a provision can be recognised?
options: A signed legal contract with a supplier
Approval of the provision by the tax authority
Certainty that only a future event will create the obligation
A present obligation arising from a past event, a probable outflow and a reliable estimate
items.explanation: IAS 37 recognises a provision only when a present obligation from a past event makes a probable outflow of economic benefits likely and the amount can be estimated reliably. Contract, tax approval and certainty about future events are not recognition criteria.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IFRS 16, how does a lessee initially account for a lease that is not a short-term or low-value lease?
options: Recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability
Expense all lease payments on a straight-line basis
Record a prepayment and recognise revenue over the term
Disclose the lease only in the notes
items.explanation: IFRS 16 requires a lessee to recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability measured at the present value of future lease payments. Straight-line expensing applies only to the recognition exemptions for short-term and low-value leases.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: A lessee enters a three-year lease with annual payments of 10,000 payable at the end of each year and an incremental borrowing rate of five per cent. The present value annuity factor is 2.723. What is the initial lease liability?
items.explanation: The initial lease liability is the present value of the future lease payments, so 10,000 multiplied by the annuity factor of 2.723 equals 27,230. Summing the undiscounted payments would overstate the liability at 30,000.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: An asset has a carrying amount of 300,000 and a tax base of 250,000, and the tax rate is 25 per cent. What deferred tax balance arises under IAS 12?
options: A deferred tax liability of 75,000
No deferred tax balance arises
A deferred tax liability of 12,500
A deferred tax asset of 12,500
items.explanation: The taxable temporary difference is 300,000 minus 250,000, which is 50,000, and 25 per cent of that is a deferred tax liability of 12,500. A liability arises because the carrying amount exceeds the tax base.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IFRS 15, when should an entity recognise revenue from a contract with a customer?
options: When the customer places the order
When the cash is received
When the invoice is issued
When the performance obligation is satisfied
items.explanation: IFRS 15 recognises revenue when control of a good or service transfers to the customer, which occurs when the performance obligation is satisfied. Order placement, cash receipt and invoicing do not by themselves transfer control.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: An entity sells goods for which the price includes a right of return within thirty days. Under IFRS 15, how should the consideration for the expected returns be treated?
options: Recognised as a refund liability with a corresponding reduction in revenue
Recognised in full as revenue with no adjustment
Deferred as a prepayment until the return period expires
Recognised as a provision for legal claims
items.explanation: IFRS 15 requires an entity to recognise expected refunds as a refund liability and to adjust revenue, while also recognising a right to recover returned goods. Recognising full revenue would overstate the transaction price.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IFRS 9, a debt instrument can be measured at amortised cost only when it passes which two tests?
options: The quoted price test and the credit loss test
The business model test and the solely payments of principal and interest test
The fair value test and the impairment test
The trading intent test and the hedging test
items.explanation: Amortised cost measurement requires the asset to be held within a business model whose objective is to collect contractual cash flows and for the cash flows to be solely payments of principal and interest. Failing either test leads to fair value measurement.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: Under IFRS 9, how should an entity measure the loss allowance for trade receivables that do not contain a significant financing component?
options: At the full carrying amount immediately
At nil until default occurs
At an amount equal to lifetime expected credit losses
At an amount equal to twelve-month expected credit losses
items.explanation: IFRS 9 permits the simplified approach, under which trade receivables without a significant financing component are measured at lifetime expected credit losses. The general twelve-month measure applies to other assets whose credit risk has not increased significantly.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements
items.stem: A fire destroys a warehouse after the reporting date but before the financial statements are authorised for issue. The warehouse existed at the reporting date. Under IAS 10, how should this event be treated?
options: As a non-adjusting event disclosed only in the notes
As a change in accounting policy applied retrospectively
As an error corrected by restating the opening equity
As an adjusting event that requires the financial statements to be adjusted
items.explanation: IAS 10 treats an event that provides evidence of conditions existing at the reporting date as an adjusting event. Because the warehouse existed at that date, the financial statements are adjusted rather than merely disclosed.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Accounting for Transactions in Financial Statements

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: An entity reports profit before interest and tax of 400,000 and total capital employed of 2,000,000. What is the return on capital employed?
options: 20 per cent
10 per cent
5 per cent
40 per cent
items.explanation: Return on capital employed is profit before interest and tax divided by capital employed, so 400,000 divided by 2,000,000 equals 20 per cent. Using profit after tax or omitting capital employed would misstate the measure.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: Revenue is 500,000 and cost of sales is 300,000. What is the gross profit margin?
options: 66.7 per cent
40 per cent
60 per cent
30 per cent
items.explanation: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of sales, which is 200,000, divided by revenue of 500,000 to give 40 per cent. The 60 per cent figure is cost of sales as a proportion of revenue.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: Current assets are 240,000, inventory is 80,000 and current liabilities are 120,000. What is the quick ratio?
items.explanation: The quick ratio excludes inventory, so 240,000 minus 80,000 equals 160,000, divided by current liabilities of 120,000 gives 1.33. Including inventory would give the current ratio of 2.00.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: Cost of sales is 600,000 and average inventory is 150,000. What is the inventory turnover period in days, using a 360-day year?
options: 120 days
60 days
36 days
90 days
items.explanation: Inventory turnover is 600,000 divided by 150,000, which is four times a year. Dividing the 360-day year by four gives a holding period of 90 days.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: Total debt is 800,000 and equity is 1,200,000. What is the gearing ratio measured as debt divided by equity?
options: 66.7 per cent
40.0 per cent
150.0 per cent
25.0 per cent
items.explanation: Gearing as debt over equity is 800,000 divided by 1,200,000, which is 66.7 per cent. Measuring debt as a proportion of total capital would give 40 per cent.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders is 300,000 and the weighted average number of ordinary shares is 500,000. What is basic earnings per share?
items.explanation: Basic earnings per share is profit attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by the weighted average number of shares, so 300,000 divided by 500,000 equals 0.60.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: An entity has profit after tax of 500,000 and pays preference dividends of 50,000. Ordinary dividends are 180,000. What is the dividend cover?
options: 2.8 times
0.36 times
2.5 times
3.6 times
items.explanation: Dividend cover is profit available to ordinary shareholders divided by ordinary dividends. Profit after deducting preference dividends is 450,000, divided by ordinary dividends of 180,000 gives 2.5 times.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: An analyst compares the ratios of two entities and finds that their accounting policies differ for inventory valuation. Which limitation of ratio analysis does this illustrate?
options: Ratios always reflect cash flows rather than profits
Ratios remove the need to read the financial statements
Ratios are unaffected by the choice of year end
Ratios can be distorted by differences in accounting policies
items.explanation: Ratio analysis is limited because policy choices such as inventory valuation, depreciation and leasing can make comparable entities appear different. Ratios summarise reported figures and do not remove policy differences.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: An entity has profit before interest and tax of 450,000 and finance costs of 90,000. What is the interest cover?
options: 5.0 times
4.0 times
0.2 times
7.5 times
items.explanation: Interest cover is profit before interest and tax divided by finance costs, so 450,000 divided by 90,000 equals 5.0 times. A higher figure indicates a greater margin of safety for lenders.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity
items.stem: An entity's return on capital employed has fallen even though profit before interest and tax has increased. Which change most likely explains this?
options: An increase in the dividend payout ratio
A larger increase in capital employed than in operating profit
A reduction in the entity's tax rate
A fall in the number of employees
items.explanation: Return on capital employed is operating profit divided by capital employed, so a fall alongside higher profit is explained by capital employed growing faster than profit. Tax, employee numbers and payout policy do not enter the numerator or denominator.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Analysing the Financial Performance of an Entity

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: When preparing a statement of cash flows using the indirect method, how should a profit on disposal of equipment be treated in the operating section?
options: Ignored entirely
Reported as a financing cash flow
Deducted from profit before tax because it is a non-operating gain
Added back to profit before tax as a non-cash item
items.explanation: The profit on disposal is included in profit before tax but arises from investing activity, so it is deducted in the operating section. The disposal proceeds themselves are shown in the investing section.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: An entity pays 200,000 to acquire a subsidiary and borrows 150,000 under a new bank loan during the year. In the statement of cash flows, how are these shown?
options: Both as operating cash flows
Both as investing cash flows
The acquisition as financing and the loan as investing
The acquisition as an investing outflow and the loan as a financing inflow
items.explanation: Acquiring a subsidiary is an investing activity, while obtaining a bank loan is a financing activity. Classifying both together would misstate the nature of the cash flows.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: An entity issues shares for cash during the year. In the statement of changes in equity, which column is affected and how?
options: Share capital and share premium increase
Retained earnings increase
Revaluation reserve increases
No equity column changes
items.explanation: Issuing shares for cash increases share capital by the nominal amount and share premium by any excess over nominal value. Retained earnings and revaluation reserves are unaffected by a share issue.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: An event after the reporting period is material and provides evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date. How should it be treated?
options: Recognise it directly in the statement of changes in equity
Adjust the amounts recognised in the financial statements
Disclose only, with no adjustment to the amounts
Apply it prospectively in the next period
items.explanation: IAS 10 requires adjusting events to be reflected in the amounts recognised in the financial statements. Non-adjusting events, which concern conditions arising after the reporting date, are disclosed only.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: An entity has earned interest revenue of 5,000 that has not yet been received at the year end. What adjustment is required in the financial statements?
options: Take the amount directly to reserves
Ignore it because cash has not been received
Recognise accrued income and increase profit
Reduce profit and create a prepayment
items.explanation: Under the accrual basis, income earned but not yet received is recognised as accrued income, increasing profit and creating a receivable. Ignoring it would understate profit and assets.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: The trial balance shows depreciation charged of 12,000, but the correct charge for the year should be 15,000. What is the effect of this error on profit for the year?
options: Profit is understated by 3,000
Profit is correct
Profit is overstated by 15,000
Profit is overstated by 3,000
items.explanation: Depreciation of 12,000 was charged instead of 15,000, so expenses are understated by 3,000 and profit is overstated by 3,000. The correcting entry increases depreciation and reduces profit.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: Under IFRS 10, which of the following is the essential basis for consolidating an investee?
options: The investor controls the investee
The investor owns more than fifty per cent of the shares
The investor has a seat on the board
The investee is registered in the same country
items.explanation: IFRS 10 requires consolidation when the investor controls the investee, meaning it has power over the relevant activities, exposure to variable returns and the ability to use its power to affect those returns. Majority ownership is an indicator but not the sole test.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: A parent acquires eighty per cent of a subsidiary for 900,000. The fair value of the subsidiary's identifiable net assets is 1,000,000 and the non-controlling interest is measured at its proportionate share. What is goodwill?
items.explanation: Goodwill is consideration of 900,000 plus the non-controlling interest of 200,000 minus net assets of 1,000,000, which gives 100,000. The NCI at proportionate share is twenty per cent of 1,000,000.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: A subsidiary had retained earnings of 200,000 at acquisition and now reports retained earnings of 350,000. The parent owns eighty per cent. What is the group share of post-acquisition retained earnings?
items.explanation: Post-acquisition retained earnings are 350,000 minus 200,000, which is 150,000. The parent's eighty per cent share is 120,000, with the remaining thirty thousand belonging to the non-controlling interest.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: A parent owns seventy-five per cent of a subsidiary whose identifiable net assets are 800,000 at the reporting date. Using the proportionate method, what is the non-controlling interest?
items.explanation: Under the proportionate method the non-controlling interest is the NCI percentage of the subsidiary's net assets, so twenty-five per cent of 800,000 equals 200,000. The parent's share is 600,000.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: A parent sells goods to its subsidiary at a profit, and some of those goods remain in the subsidiary's inventory at the year end. What adjustment is required in the consolidation?
options: Eliminate the unrealised profit against group retained earnings and inventory
Eliminate only the intra-group sale, leaving inventory at cost
Recognise the profit as a gain in the group accounts
Increase group inventory to the selling price
items.explanation: The unrealised profit on goods still held within the group is removed by reducing inventory and group retained earnings, with part allocated to the non-controlling interest. Recognising it would overstate group profit and assets.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: At the reporting date a parent has a receivable of 50,000 due from its subsidiary and the subsidiary has a corresponding payable. How are these balances treated in the consolidated statement of financial position?
options: They are reclassified as equity
They are cancelled against each other and not reported
They are shown separately as a receivable and a payable
Only the receivable is reported
items.explanation: Intra-group balances are eliminated on consolidation so that the group does not report a receivable from and payable to itself. Showing them separately would inflate both assets and liabilities.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: Under IAS 28, how should an investment in an associate be accounted for in the group financial statements?
options: By full consolidation line by line
At fair value through profit or loss in all cases
Using the equity method
At cost less impairment only
items.explanation: IAS 28 requires associates, over which the investor has significant influence, to be accounted for using the equity method. Full consolidation is reserved for subsidiaries, and cost or fair value treatment applies only in limited circumstances.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: An investor owns thirty per cent of an associate that reports profit after tax of 200,000 and pays total dividends of 40,000. What amount is recognised as the investor's share of the associate's profit?
items.explanation: The investor recognises its share of the associate's profit after tax, so thirty per cent of 200,000 equals 60,000. Dividends received reduce the carrying amount of the investment rather than being recognised as income.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: Group retained earnings equal the parent's retained earnings plus the group share of post-acquisition retained earnings of subsidiaries. Which item is also deducted where relevant?
options: The parent's share of unrealised profit on intra-group inventory
The non-controlling interest share of pre-acquisition profits
The subsidiary's share capital at acquisition
The parent's dividend paid to shareholders
items.explanation: Group retained earnings are reduced by the parent's share of unrealised profit on intra-group sales still held in inventory. Pre-acquisition profits are excluded from the post-acquisition movement, and share capital is a separate component of equity.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)

items.domain: Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
items.stem: Under IFRS 3, which of the following may be measured either at fair value or at the proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets?
options: The acquiree's identifiable liabilities
The non-controlling interest at the acquisition date
Goodwill arising on consolidation
The consideration transferred by the acquirer
items.explanation: IFRS 3 allows the non-controlling interest at the acquisition date to be measured either at fair value or at the non-controlling interest's proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets. Goodwill and consideration are measured at fair value.
items.reference: ACCA FR Syllabus Study Guide - Preparation of Financial Statements (Including Consolidated)
